claims.evidence: Cited from Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2015

claims.claim: Both atypical and classical MBCs from malaria patients are capable of secreting antibodies against blood-stage P. falciparum antigens
claims.source: Although the unresponsiveness of these cells to direct ex-vivo stimulation with different standard stimuli suggested that these cells were inactive (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017), both atypical and classical MBCs from malaria patients are capable of secreting antibodies against blood-stage P. falciparum antigens (Krishnamurty et al., 2016; Lugaajju et al., 2017; Muellenbeck et al., 2013; Portugal et al., 2017) (Kim et al., 2019; Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2018; Sundling et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple sources including Krishnamurty et al., 2016; Lugaajju et al., 2017; Muellenbeck et al., 2013; Portugal et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019; Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2018; Sundling et al., 2019

claims.claim: Atypical MBCs in Plasmodium-infected mice are short-lived and do not contribute to the long-lived anti-malaria immune response
claims.source: Atypical MBCs have also been described in Plasmodium-infected mice, where they were characterized as short-lived, and therefore not contributing to the long-lived anti malaria immune response (Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2018)

claims.claim: Atypical MBCs in Plasmodium-infected mice limit the protective anti-parasite antibody response
claims.source: Atypical MBCs have also been described in Plasmodium-infected mice, where they were characterized as short-lived, and therefore not contributing to the long-lived anti malaria immune response (Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2018), but where they were able to limit the protective anti-parasite antibody response (Guthmiller et al., 2017).

claims.claim: T-bet+ B-cells are the main producers of anti-PS IgG antibodies during malarial anemia in mice
claims.source: In our previous study in mice, we characterized T-bet+ B-cells as the main producers of anti-PS IgG antibodies during malarial anemia (Rivera-Correa et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The correlation of expansion of atypical MBCs with anemia in patients suggests that these cells have a role in malaria pathogenesis
claims.source: The correlation of expansion of atypical MBCs with anemia in patients suggests that these cells have a role in malaria pathogenesis, providing clinical significance to our findings.
claims.evidence: Inference from correlation data presented in the study

claims.claim: T-bet+ B-cells in mice are activated directly by Plasmodium DNA through TLR-9 alongside IFN-γ to produce anti-PS antibodies
claims.source: T-bet+ B-cells in these mice are activated directly by Plasmodium DNA through TLR-9 alongside IFN-γ to produce anti-PS antibodies (Rivera-Correa et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Atypical T-bet+FcRL5+ memory B-cells contribute to malarial anemia in P. falciparum-infected patients through anti-PS antibody secretion
claims.source: Collectively, results from the analysis of patient samples and from in vitro stimulation of healthy PBMC, suggest that atypical T-bet+FcRL5+ memory B-cells contribute to malarial anemia in P.-falciparum-infected patients through anti-PS antibody secretion.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from patient samples and in vitro experiments

claims.claim: Atypical T-bet+FcRL5+ B-cells are major promoters of autoimmune-mediated malaria anemia in P. falciparum infections
claims.source: In summary, our results provide the first mechanistic evidence of autoimmune-mediated malaria anemia in patients, and suggest that atypical T-bet+FcRL5+ B-cells are major promoters of this pathology in P.-falciparum-infections.

claims.claim: The study cohort consisted of 24 P. falciparum-infected patients with 31 unique samples
claims.source: In this study, we focused on samples (24 patients, 31 unique samples) from a cohort of P.-falciparum-infected returned travelers from Germany, who acquired malaria while visiting Africa.

claims.claim: The P. falciparum strain 3D7 was used for in vitro culture experiments
claims.source: Erythrocyte asexual stage cultures of the P. falciparum strain 3D7 were maintained at 5% hematocrit in RPMI 1640

claims.claim: Ionomycin treatment at 2.5 µM induces PS exposure in erythrocytes
claims.source: First, fresh healthy donor erythrocytes were treated with ionomycin at 2.5 µM (Life Technologies) to stress erythrocytes and to induce exposure of PS (Lang et al., 2006).

claims.claim: The expression of T-bet is significantly higher in FcRL5+ cells compared to classical MBCs
claims.source: To define the atypical and classical MBC populations better, we analyzed the expression of T-bet in FcRL5+ cells compared to classical MBCs, finding that the expression of T-bet is significantly higher in FcRL5+ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

results.result: Malaria remains a major global health threat with over 200 million infections and 400,000 deaths in 2017, with anemia being a common and significant complication contributing to morbidity and mortality.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are all supported by citations to authoritative sources (WHO 2018, White 2018). These are well-established epidemiological facts about malaria burden and its complications, appropriately cited from the literature.

results.result: Malarial anemia has a multi-factorial etiology involving clearance of both infected and uninfected erythrocytes and bone marrow dyserythropoiesis, with approximately 8 uninfected erythrocytes killed per infected cell in P. falciparum and 34 in P. vivax infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Lamikanra et al., 2007; White, 2018; Jakeman et al., 1999; Price et al., 2001; Collins et al., 2003). These represent established knowledge about malaria pathophysiology.

results.result: While anti-parasite B-cell antibody responses are essential for protective immunity, autoantibodies also mediate malaria pathologies, specifically anti-phosphatidylserine antibodies that promote anemia in mouse models and correlate with low hemoglobin in malaria patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C12 are supported by appropriate citations establishing both the protective role of anti-parasite antibodies and the pathological role of autoantibodies, particularly anti-PS antibodies. The mouse model data and patient correlations are properly cited from prior work.

results.result: T-bet+ B-cells, which secrete autoantibodies in autoimmune mouse models and are major producers of anti-PS antibodies in mouse malaria, have been identified in malaria-endemic populations as atypical memory B-cells characterized by low antibody secretion and inhibitory markers like FcRL5.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature establishing the role of T-bet+ B-cells in autoimmunity and malaria, and their characterization as atypical memory B-cells. This provides the necessary background for the current study.

results.result: The cohort of P. falciparum-infected German returned travelers exhibited mild anemia with hemoglobin levels below normal ranges, and hemoglobin did not correlate with parasitemia, confirming that direct erythrocyte infection is not a major cause of anemia.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 are supported by data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1A. The lack of correlation between hemoglobin and parasitemia is consistent with prior studies (cited) and supports the multi-factorial nature of malarial anemia. The statistical analysis appears appropriate.

results.result: Anti-PS IgG antibodies and anti-erythrocyte IgG antibodies inversely correlate with hemoglobin levels in P. falciparum patients, while anti-PfEBA and anti-DNA antibodies do not, suggesting specificity of the autoimmune response contributing to anemia.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 and C27 are supported by correlation data shown in Figures 1B, 1C, 1D, and 1E. The statistical analyses show significant correlations for anti-PS and anti-erythrocyte antibodies but not for anti-PfEBA or anti-DNA antibodies, supporting the specificity of the autoimmune response. The use of Spearman correlation is appropriate for this data.

results.result: Anti-erythrocyte antibodies recognize all kinds of antigens in human erythrocyte lysates, including PS.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by citations to prior work (Mourão et al., 2018; Mourão et al., 2016) characterizing the broad specificity of anti-erythrocyte antibodies.

results.result: Anti-PS IgG antibodies correlate with LDH levels and erythrocyte lysis capacity in P. falciparum patient plasma, with plasma from patients being more effective at lysing PS-exposing erythrocytes than control plasma, and this lysis is partially reduced by annexin V pre-treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are supported by data in Figure 2A-D. The correlations between anti-PS antibodies and LDH (C31) and lysis capacity (C33) are statistically significant. The in vitro lysis assay (C32) shows significant differences between patient and control plasma. The partial reduction by annexin V (C34) supports PS-specificity while acknowledging other antibody specificities may contribute. The experimental design and controls are appropriate.

results.result: Annexin V specifically binds to PS and inhibits the binding of anti-PS antibodies.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by appropriate citations (Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016; van Engeland et al., 1998) establishing the specificity of annexin V for PS and its ability to block anti-PS antibody binding.

results.result: FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells are significantly expanded in PBMC from P. falciparum-infected German returned travelers compared to uninfected controls, with no significant differences between tourist and VFR groups or between genders.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B and supplementary figures. The expansion of FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells is highly significant (p≤0.0001). The lack of differences by patient background or gender is appropriately documented. The gating strategy appears sound.

results.result: Time after treatment does not correlate with hemoglobin levels but shows a significant direct correlation with atypical MBC levels, suggesting these cells continue to increase after treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by data from the patient cohort (Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3). The correlation analysis is appropriate, though the interpretation that cells 'continue to increase' (C40) is somewhat speculative and could reflect ongoing activation rather than continued proliferation.

results.result: Atypical MBCs inversely correlate with hemoglobin levels and positively correlate with patient age, but do not correlate with parasitemia or thrombocyte counts. Classical memory B-cells and plasma cells positively correlate with hemoglobin levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 are supported by correlation data in Figure 4 and supplementary figures. The inverse correlation between atypical MBCs and hemoglobin (C41) is statistically significant and represents a key finding. The lack of correlation with parasitemia (C42) and thrombocytes (C44) supports specificity for anemia. The positive correlations of classical MBCs (C45) and plasma cells (C46) with hemoglobin provide important contrasts. The age correlation (C43) is consistent with prior literature on age-associated B-cells.

results.result: T-bet expression is significantly higher in FcRL5+ cells compared to classical MBCs.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing significantly higher T-bet expression in FcRL5+ cells (p≤0.01). This validates the characterization of these cells as atypical MBCs.

results.result: FcRL5+T-bet+ atypical MBCs positively correlate with anti-PS IgG antibodies while classical MBCs inversely correlate with anti-PS antibodies. Naïve, immature, and plasma cells do not correlate with anti-PS antibodies. Classical and atypical MBCs show a significant negative correlation with each other.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are supported by correlation data in Figure 5 and supplementary figures. The positive correlation between atypical MBCs and anti-PS antibodies (C47) is a key finding linking these cells to autoantibody production. The inverse correlation with classical MBCs (C48) and the negative correlation between the two MBC populations (C52) are statistically significant. The lack of correlations with other B-cell subsets (C49-C51) supports specificity.

results.result: FcRL5+T-bet+ atypical MBCs and plasma cells positively correlate with anti-erythrocyte IgG antibodies in P. falciparum patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by correlation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The positive correlation with atypical MBCs resembles the anti-PS pattern, while the correlation with plasma cells suggests these cells may produce other autoantibodies besides anti-PS.

results.result: Anti-DNA antibodies do not correlate with atypical MBCs in P. falciparum patients.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by correlation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3. The lack of correlation suggests anti-DNA antibodies are not predominantly produced by atypical MBCs, supporting the specificity of these cells for anti-PS and anti-erythrocyte antibodies.

results.result: Anti-PfEBA IgG antibodies do not significantly correlate with any B-cell subsets in P. falciparum patients.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by correlation data in Figure 6. The lack of correlation between anti-parasite antibodies and any B-cell subset, including atypical MBCs, contrasts with the strong correlations seen for autoantibodies and supports the specificity of atypical MBCs for autoantibody production.

results.result: FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells expand robustly when PBMC from healthy donors are stimulated with P. falciparum-infected erythrocyte lysates. FcRL5+-enriched cells show significantly more anti-PS-specific B-cells than CD27+-enriched cells, with similar numbers of anti-PfEBA-specific cells in both populations. CD27+-enriched cells have higher total antibody-secreting cells than FcRL5+ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by data in Figure 7A-B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The in vitro expansion of FcRL5+T-bet+ cells (C57) and the ELISPOT data showing enrichment of anti-PS-specific cells in the FcRL5+ population (C58) provide direct evidence that these cells produce anti-PS antibodies. The similar numbers of anti-PfEBA cells (C59) and higher total ASCs in CD27+ cells (C60) are important controls showing that FcRL5+ cells are specifically enriched for anti-PS production.

results.result: Stimulation with P. falciparum HRPII or uninfected erythrocyte lysate does not induce significant expansion of FcRL5+T-bet+ cells, consistent with the requirement for B-cell receptor stimulation, inflammatory cytokines (IFNγ/IL-21), and Plasmodium DNA for optimal expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior work (Phalke and Marrack, 2018; Rivera-Correa et al., 2017). The lack of expansion with HRPII or uninfected lysate provides important negative controls and supports the mechanistic explanation for why infected lysates are required.

results.result: Atypical FcRL5+T-bet+ B-cells produce anti-PS antibodies upon stimulation with parasite lysates in vitro and contribute to malarial anemia in P. falciparum-infected patients through anti-PS antibody secretion, representing the first mechanistic evidence of autoimmune-mediated malaria anemia in patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 and C76-C77 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating findings from patient correlations and in vitro experiments. The evidence from multiple complementary approaches (correlations between atypical MBCs, anti-PS antibodies, and anemia; in vitro demonstration of anti-PS production by FcRL5+ cells; functional lysis assays) provides strong support for these conclusions. However, the causal language ('contribute to,' 'major promoters') is somewhat stronger than what correlation data alone can support, though the in vitro functional data strengthens the case.

results.result: T-bet+ B-cells have been studied in autoimmunity and malaria contexts, with prior work establishing their role in autoantibody production in mouse models and their expansion in malaria-endemic populations as atypical MBCs with reduced ex vivo function but capability to secrete anti-parasite antibodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C75 provide background context from prior literature and are supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the foundation for the current study's investigation of atypical MBCs in malaria patients.

results.result: The study used a cohort of 24 P. falciparum-infected patients (31 samples) from Germany, P. falciparum strain 3D7 for in vitro experiments, and ionomycin treatment to induce PS exposure on erythrocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 describe methodological details that are appropriately documented in the Materials and Methods section and supported by citations where relevant (e.g., Lang et al., 2006 for ionomycin-induced PS exposure).

results.result: Anti-DNA antibodies are typical in autoimmune diseases.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 is supported by citation to Tsokos, 2011, establishing this as general knowledge about autoimmune diseases.
